title: See's Candies — $25M purchase becomes the template for pricing power
statement: Paid $25M for a West-Coast box-chocolates business earning roughly $4M pre-tax, betting on brand-driven pricing power rather than asset value.
outcome: Generated over $2 billion cumulative pre-tax earnings in the decades after purchase, and taught the intangibles lesson that shaped every later Berkshire acquisition.

title: Washington Post — bought fear in a family-controlled franchise
statement: Bought about 10% of the Post's business class when the market priced the whole company far below liquidation estimates, despite an entrenched controlling family.
outcome: Position grew more than tenfold over two decades; Buffett later called the price 'a huge bargain' and held the stake until Graham Holdings converted in 2014.

title: GEICO rescue — doubling down when insolvency headlines peaked
statement: Backed a near-insolvent insurer because its core low-cost direct model remained intact, starting accumulation at depressed prices while others fled.
outcome: Became Berkshire's float engine; the position was eventually bought out entirely and remains a core subsidiary half a century later.

title: Salomon Brothers — $700M convertible preferred at the bottom of a cycle
statement: Deployed $700M into a redeemable convertible preferred when the firm needed capital, accepting governance risk for yield-plus-upside terms.
outcome: Preferred was redeemed after the 1990s; the episode produced both gains and a famous governance headache Buffett chronicled in subsequent letters.

title: Coca-Cola — the definitive permanent holding
statement: Accumulated roughly 7% of Coca-Cola across 1988–1994 for about $1.3B total, paying up for an unambiguous global brand rather than waiting for deep-value prices.
outcome: Never sold; dividends alone came to exceed the original cost basis annually within three decades, making it Berkshire's textbook example of compounding brand equity.

title: GEICO — acquiring the remaining 50% outright
statement: Bought the half of GEICO Berkshire didn't already own for $2.3B, converting a famous partial position into wholly-owned float.
outcome: GEICO grew policies and float multiples over; became one of Berkshire's largest and most strategic operating units.

title: General Re — the $22B reinsurance bet and its hard lesson
statement: Acquired General Re for ~$22B in stock, instantly gaining one of the world's largest reinsurers along with its underwriting culture.
outcome: Early years exposed unpriced derivative exposure and inadequate reserves that took years to fix — a candid multi-letter case study in integration risk before it became a strong underwriting business.

title: Goldman Sachs preferred — liquidity for trust at the panic lows
statement: Invested $5B in 10% dividend-paying preferred shares plus warrants during the crisis, explicitly saying confidence in the institution mattered as much as terms.
outcome: Redeemed in 2011 with a premium; overall profit ran to billions, cementing the crisis-preferred playbook.

title: BNSF — the largest acquisition in Berkshire history
statement: Acquired the remaining ~77% of Burlington Northern Santa Fe in a deal valuing the railroad at about $34B including assumed debt, calling it an all-in wager on the American economy.
outcome: BNSF became Berkshire's largest non-insurance earner and the backbone of domestic freight logistics; earnings and reinvestment both scaled dramatically.

title: IBM — a rare public miss
statement: Built a ~$10.7B stake convinced by long client relationships and capital discipline, publicly writing up the thesis in that year's shareholder letter.
outcome: Business trajectory disappointed; by 2017 Buffett wrote plainly that results fell short of his original expectations and Berkshire had exited at roughly break-even.

title: Precision Castparts — paying too much for quality
statement: Closed the ~$32B acquisition of aerospace-parts maker Precision Castparts, Berkshire's largest cash acquisition at the time.
outcome: Aerospace demand collapsed after COVID and normalized earnings proved well below what was paid for; Buffett said directly he paid too much.

title: Apple — concentration into the best business he ever bought
statement: Started buying Apple in 2016 and scaled aggressively through 2018, treating it as a consumer-products company with unmatched ecosystem retention rather than a tech bet.
outcome: Grew into the most profitable single investment in Berkshire's history, worth multiples of its ~$36B cost basis and generating enormous annual dividends.

title: Airlines — full exit within weeks of the crash
statement: Sold the entire four-airline position in April 2020 after concluding the world had changed for aviation economics, reversing a thesis built over years.
outcome: A candid, immediate reversal executed at scale — later cited by Buffett himself as an error in judgment made quickly rather than stubbornly defended.

title: Japan sogo shosha — five 5% stakes at historically cheap yields
statement: Accumulated just over 5% in each of Japan's five major trading houses, attracted by extraordinarily low valuations, dividend cultures, and aligned management.
outcome: Positions were raised over time and became one of Berkshire's best-performing commitments of the decade, praised in the 2023 letter for their capital discipline.
